'''William Charles Waterhouse''' (December 31, 1941 – June 26, 2016) was an American [[mathematician]]. He was a [[professor emeritus]] of Mathematics at [[Pennsylvania State University]],<ref name="dir-emer"/> after having taught there for over 35 years.<ref name="ams-miniobit">{{cite news | url=http://www.ams.org/news?news_id=3159 | title=News from the AMS: William C. 'Bill' Waterhouse (1941&ndash;2016) | publisher=American Mathematical Society | date=September 6, 2016 | access-date=March 15, 2023}}</ref> The early part of his career was at [[Cornell University]].<ref name="ams-miniobit"/> His research interests included [[abstract algebra]], [[number theory]], [[group scheme]]s, and the [[history of mathematics]].<ref name="dir">[http://www.math.psu.edu/directory/faculty.php PSU Mathematics Department – Faculty], retrieved 2010-02-06.</ref>

==Early life and education==
Waterhouse was born in [[Galveston, Texas]], on December 31, 1941, the son of William T. Waterhouse and Grace D. Waterhouse,<ref name="CDT"/> but grew up in [[Denver, Colorado]].<ref name="tf-proofs">{{cite journal | url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/07468342.1989.11973231 | title=Two Elementary Proofs of an Inequality (and 1½ Better Ones) | author-first=William C. | author-last=Waterhouse | journal=The College Mathematics Journal | volume=20 | number=3 | pages= 201&ndash;205 | doi= 10.1080/07468342.1989.11973231 | year=1989 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>  His father was an engineer who was employed with the [[United States Bureau of Reclamation]].<ref name="time-800s"/>

He attended [[East High School (Denver, Colorado)|East High School]] in Denver.<ref name="dp-contest"/> In a high school mathematics competition spanning the states of Colorado, South Dakota, and Wyoming, he received the highest score in the competition's history and helped his school gain the top mark.<ref name="dp-contest">{{cite news | url=https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/william-c-waterhouse-east-high-school-senior-demonstrates-news-photo/837073128 | title=uncertain | newspaper=The Denver Post | date=March 25, 1959 | page= }}</ref> As a senior, he took the [[Scholastic Aptitude Test]] and received a near-perfect 797 on the verbal portion and a perfect 800 on the math portion.<ref name="time-800s"/> He then received perfect 800 scores on three different college board [[Achievement Tests]], those [[Achievement Test in English Composition|for English Composition]], [[Achievement Test in Chemistry|for Chemistry]], and [[Achievement Test in Mathematics Level II|for advanced Mathematics]],<ref name="time-800s"/> a feat that the [[Associated Press]] filed a story about and that ran in a number of newspapers around the country.<ref name="ap-800s">See for example {{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/102964799/attendance-figures-for-busch-gardens/ | title=Flawless Performance | agency=Associated Press | newspaper=The Tampa Times | date=June 13, 1959 | page=2-C | via=Newspapers.com}} Newspapers.com shows [https://www.newspapers.com/search/?query=%22william%20c.%20waterhouse%22%20%22800%20scores%22%20%22east%20high%20school%22&dr_year=1959-1959 over fifty papers] running the AP report.</ref>  <!-- westinghouse contest honors group, not sure what means, leave out probably
https://www.newspapers.com/image/24977497/?terms=%22william%20charles%20waterhouse%22&match=1 -->  ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine ran a profile of him as well.<ref name="time-800s">{{cite news | url=https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,811057,00.html | title=Education: The Good Student | magazine=Time | date=April 27, 1959 }}</ref>  Waterhouse received the [[National Merit Scholarship]] and the General Motors Scholarship;<ref name="time-800s"/> he graduated from East High in 1959.<ref name="dp-contest"/>

Waterhouse attended [[Harvard College]].  There he was a standout in the [[Putnam Competition]]:<!-- https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/Putnam/Competition_Archive/List%20of%20Previous%20Putnam%20Winners.pdf --> As a sophomore in the 1960 competition, he was not part of Harvard's three-person team that finished second overall, but he did achieve a top-ten individual mark;<ref>{{cite journal | author-last=Bush | author-first=L. E. | title=The 1960 William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition | journal=The American Mathematical Monthly | volume=68 | number= 7 | year=1961 | pages= 629&ndash;637 | doi=10.2307/2311508 | jstor=2311508 }}</ref> as a junior in the 1961 competition, he attained the highest individual level &ndash; a top-five score &ndash; while helping his Harvard team to a fourth-place finish overall;<ref>{{cite journal | author-last=Bush | author-first= L. E. | title=The 1961 William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition | journal= The American Mathematical Monthly | volume=69 | number= 8 | year=1962 |pages= 759&ndash;767 | doi=10.2307/2310772 | jstor= 2310772 }}</ref> and as a senior in the 1962 competition, he again was a Putnam Fellow with a top-five score and helped his Harvard team to a third-place finish overall.<ref name="hc-1963">{{cite news | url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1963/3/16/three-math-students-win-third-in/ | title=Three Math Students Win Third in Contest | newspaper=The Harvard Crimson | date=March 16, 1963 }}</ref>

After graduating from Harvard College with a bachelor's degree ''summa cum laude'' and  being elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]], Waterhouse continued at [[Harvard Graduate School of Arts and Sciences]] where he received a master's degree.<ref name="cdt-2math"/>  While in the graduate school, he was awarded a [[NSF-GRFP|National Science Foundation Fellowship]].<ref name="cdt-2math"/>  He then received his Ph.D. in 1968 from Harvard for his thesis ''Abelian Varieties over Finite Fields'' under the supervision of [[John Tate (mathematician)|John Tate]].<ref name="lrf84"/>

==Career==
[[Image:Cornell University notebook and exam pages for Math 221, Spring 1973.jpg|thumb|right|Student's notebook pages from a 1973 calculus class at Cornell showing Waterhouse illustrating the applicability of Fourier series to music theory by singing notes and commenting on their harmonics]]
Waterhouse began teaching at Cornell University in 1968.<ref name="CDT"/>

He had a career-long interest in the history of mathematics,<ref name="dir"/> and while at Cornell wrote a history of the early years of that university's Oliver Club, a discussion forum begun by pioneering Cornell mathematician [[James Edward Oliver]] in the 1890s.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://math.cornell.edu/about-oliver-club | title=About the Oliver Club  | publisher=Department of Mathematics, Cornell University | access-date=February 8, 2023}}</ref>

Waterhouse remained an [[assistant professor]] at Cornell until 1975, at which point he was appointed an [[associate professor]] at Penn State.<!-- these two clauses tell the story  --><ref name="cdt-2math">{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/116094841/ | title=2 Named in Mathematics | newspaper=Centre Daily Times | location=State College, Pennsylvania | date=September 10, 1975 | page=20 | via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>  At Penn State, he subsequently became a [[full professor]].<ref name="tf-proofs"/>

<!-- engagement notice, nothing really new https://www.newspapers.com/image/114285850/?terms=%22william%20c.%20waterhouse%22%20%22mathematics%22&match=1 -->In 1980 he married Betty Ann Senk, a doctoral student and teacher in comparative literature at Penn State.<ref name="cdt-marriage">{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/116136811/ | title=Senk&ndash;Waterhouse Marriage | newspaper=Centre Daily Times | location=State College, Pennsylvania | date=October 17, 1980 | page=10 | via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>  They lived in [[State College, Pennsylvania]].<ref name="cdt-marriage"/>

According to his obituary published in the ''[[Centre Daily Times]]'',  during his career Waterhouse published over 250 articles in scholarly journals and other publications.<ref name="CDT"/> He was the author of the 1979 textbook ''Introduction to Affine Group Schemes'' for [[Springer-Verlag]].<ref>Graduate Texts in Mathematics 66, Springer-Verlag, 1979, {{ISBN|978-0-387-90421-4}}.</ref>  [[Telegraphic Reviews]] characterized the work as a "fairly intuitive and accessible" development of the topic, suitable for second-year graduate students.<ref>{{cite journal | title=Telegraphic Reviews | journal= The American Mathematical Monthly | volume=87 | number= 3 | date=1980 | pages= 233–238 | jstor= 2321635 | url= http://www.jstor.org/stable/2321635 }}</ref> In a 1986 volume for Springer-Verlag, he edited the 1966 translation by Arthur A. Clarke of  [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]]'s ''[[Disquisitiones Arithmeticae]]''.<ref>Reprinted in 1986 by Springer-Verlag, {{ISBN|978-0-387-96254-2}}.</ref> Waterhouse and his wife collaborated on several translations of works by German mathematicians.<ref>{{cite book | chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4RgwEAAAQBAJ&pg=PT23 | title=Arguing with Numbers: The Intersections of Rhetoric and Mathematics | author-first=James | author-last=Wynn | author2-first=G. Mitchell | author2-last=Reyes | editor-first=James | editor-last=Wynn |  editor2-first=G. Mitchell | editor2-last=Reyes | year=2021 | publisher=Pennsylvania State University Press | page=23 | chapter=From Division to Multiplication: Uncovering the Relationship Between Mathematics and Rhetoric Through Transdisciplinary Scholarship| isbn=978-0-271-08921-8 }} also {{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bQVDDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA317 | title=Rational Points on Varieties | author-first= Bjorn | author-last=Poonen | publisher=American Mathematical Society | location=Providence, Rhode Island | year=2017 | page=317 | isbn=978-1-4704-3773-2 }} <!-- also
https://books.google.com/books?id=C-Ka_POo9F8C&pg=PA195, duplicates the second one --></ref> He was a member of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] and the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref name="cdt-2math"/>

Waterhouse long had an interest in [[classical studies]];<ref name="CDT"/> as such, he was a member of the [[Classical Association of the Middle West and South]].<ref>{{cite conference | url=https://camws.org/sites/default/files/Program2019.pdf | title=Program: 115th Annual CAMWS Meeting | location=Lincoln, Nebraska | date=2019 | page=69 | contribution=CAMWS Necrology | publisher=Classical Association of the Middle West and South}}</ref>  He published a number of entries about language- and classics-focused matters in the journal ''[[Notes and Queries]]'',<ref>See [https://academic.oup.com/nq/search-results?page=1&q=%22william%20c.%20waterhouse%22&fl_SiteID=5224&SearchSourceType=1&allJournals=1 search results at ''Notes and Queries'' archive], accessed March 10, 2023.</ref> as well as, in the journal ''[[Classical World (journal)|Classical World]]'',  an exegesis  of an unusual word form found in [[Ovid]]'s ''[[Amores (Ovid)|Amores]]''.<ref>{{cite journal | author-last=Waterhouse | author-first=William C. | title=''Emodulanda'' in Ovid's ''Amores'' 1.1 | journal=Classical World | volume=101 | number= 4 | date=2008 | pages= 533&ndash;534 | doi=10.1353/clw.0.0027 | url=https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/72/article/247168 | via=Project Muse| url-access=subscription }}</ref>  Waterhouse also had an interest in investigating quotations, whether via a [[Usenet]] newsgroup or publishing with [[The Skeptics Society]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.skeptic.com/eskeptic/06-01-05/ | title=Did Einstein Praise the Church? | author-first=William C. | author-last=Waterhouse | work=eSkeptic | publisher=The Skeptics Society | date=January 5, 2006 | access-date=March 15, 2023}}</ref>

By 2012,<!-- per archive.org, was still regular status in 2008, but 2009-11 are shielded by a recaptcha --> Waterhouse had moved to emeritus status.<ref name="dir-emer">{{cite web | url=http://www.math.psu.edu/directory/emeriti.php | title=Mathematics Department: Emeriti | publisher=Pennsylvania State University | access-date=March 15, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121030061237/http://www.math.psu.edu/directory/emeriti.php | archive-date=October 30, 2012}}</ref>

Waterhouse died on June 26, 2016, in State College, Pennsylvania.<ref name="CDT">{{cite news|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/centredaily/obituary.aspx?pid=180493353|title=William C. Waterhouse Obituary|newspaper=Centre Daily Times|date=June 29, 2016|access-date=April 21, 2022}}. Also available [https://camws.org/node/1051 at this CAMWS page].</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Waterhouse twice won the [[Lester R. Ford Award]] of the [[Mathematical Association of America]], given to authors of articles of expository excellence.  The first was in 1984 for his paper "Do Symmetric Problems Have Symmetric Solutions?"<ref name="lrf84">{{cite web | url=http://mathdl.maa.org/mathDL/22/?pa=content&sa=viewDocument&nodeId=2941 | title=MAA Writing Awards: Do Symmetric Problems Have Symmetric Solutions? | publisher=Mathematical Association of America | access-date=February 7, 2010}}</ref><!-- 1984 award, nothing really new https://www.newspapers.com/image/755568961/?terms=%22william%20c.%20waterhouse%22%20%22penn%20state%22&match=1 --> and the second was in 1995 for his paper "A Counterexample for Germain".<ref>{{cite web | url=http://mathdl.maa.org/mathDL/22/?pa=content&sa=viewDocument&nodeId=2910 | title=MAA Writing Awards: A Counterexample for Germain | publisher=Mathematical Association of America | access-date=February 7, 2010}}</ref> The latter has been characterized as "a historical and mathematical detective story" that investigated an aspect of the correspondence between 
[[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] and [[Sophie Germain]], a French mathematician who used a pseudonym to disguise the fact  that she was a woman.<ref name="cdt-1995">{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/120230164/ | title=Penn State Briefs: Math Professor Wins Award | newspaper=Centre Daily Times | date=August 21, 1995 | page=3 | via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> According to his obituary, Waterhouse had a special pride in having won the two Lester R. Ford Awards.<ref name="CDT"/>
